\chapter{El Libro Que Compre --- The Word You Cannot Leave Out}
\label{ch:relative-obligatory}
\hlchaptermodality{187}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can supply the que that English deletes.}

Complete ES-C53-que-no-se-cae: produce el libro que compre and name the English pattern that always needs a que.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el libro que compré]{el libro que compré — the word you cannot leave out}

\label{lesson:ES-C53-que-no-se-cae}



\begin{quote}
Say this English sentence out loud: \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}the book I bought.\textquotedblright{}} Notice that you did not say \emph{that}. Now try to translate it.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: English drops it, Spanish never does}]
\begin{quote}
\emph{el libro \textbf{que} compré} — the book I bought. \emph{la casa \textbf{que} tengo} — the house I have.
\end{quote}

English lets you delete the joint. \emph{The book that I bought} and \emph{the book I bought} are both fine, and in speech you almost always drop it.

\textbf{Spanish cannot.} There is no version of these without \emph{que}. Leaving it out does not sound casual or fast — it sounds like a sentence that broke.

This is worth a chapter of its own because of what it does to a learner. You will build the sentence in English first, silently, with the \emph{that} already missing — and then translate the version you thought of. The gap is invisible precisely because your own language put it there.

\textbf{So the habit to build is: whenever an English noun is followed straight by a new subject and verb, a \emph{que} belongs in the Spanish.}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the book \textbf{I} bought $\to$ \emph{el libro \textbf{que} compré}
  \item the house \textbf{we} have $\to$ \emph{la casa \textbf{que} tenemos}
  \item the meal \textbf{she} makes $\to$ \emph{la comida \textbf{que} hace}
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
English can afford to drop it because its word order is rigid: \emph{the book I bought} can only be read one way.

Spanish word order is looser — subjects vanish under pro-drop, objects move in front of verbs. Where the pieces can sit in several places, a deletable joint would make sentences ambiguous. So it is never deleted. Not arbitrary strictness: the price of the freedom Spanish gives you elsewhere.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}the book I bought\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}el libro que compré\textquotedblright{} — hear the extra word
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} Until the missing English \emph{that} stops being invisible.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\textquotedblleft{}The house I have\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{La casa que tengo}}.) Can \emph{que} ever be left out? (\textbf{No} — never.) And why not? (Because Spanish \textbf{moves its pieces around}, so the joint has to stay.)
\end{tcolorbox}
